cells.tense: You are standing here with the pen, and the choice you make will be the one you keep.
cells.ask: Pick the direction you have already proven, say it out loud, set it where you'll see it, and let one finished piece leave the table today.
cells.core:
You're the one at the table deciding what gets chosen. Your method isn't the loudest thing in the room — it's the proven one. You test a thing, you keep what held, and you decide from that steadiness, not from how you feel about it that morning.

That authority comes from all the hours behind it. People can feel when a decision has been worked through, and they follow it. Keep the method clean and it will keep carrying weight. What this balance is free to feed is the next build — the version of this where ground you've tested becomes ground something else stands on.
cells.sheetLine: You choose by method, and the choice holds.
cells.verb: deciding by method, committing to the answer your own practice has already tested
cells.place: at a worktable where a direction gets chosen and held

cells.tense: You are bracing for a version of this that hasn't arrived yet, and the bracing is spending today.
cells.ask: Take one question you keep answering ahead of time, write it down open, and leave it unanswered until tomorrow.
cells.core:
You're deciding ahead of the evidence. Every open question gets an answer before it has earned one, and you're living in an argument you keep winning in advance. The thinking that used to make things clear has turned into defense.

When this sits right, practice runs without force. You go quiet with a problem, the quiet connects you to the work instead of walling you off, and the refining serves the thing itself rather than your worry about it. That's the version to aim at. Your method isn't built to answer the future — it settles what's in front of you, and it's very good at that. Loosen the grip on what hasn't happened and the same discipline goes back to being a tool instead of a shift that runs all night.
cells.sheetLine: You're answering questions that haven't been asked yet.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you, and you haven't turned around to see it.
cells.ask: Ask one person what you're actually good at, take the answer without arguing, and use it to pick a small thing to commit to this week.
cells.core:
At the worktable you knew something and you're not bringing it forward. The committing stopped; what you'd proven didn't. You're treating a situation as still open that has already resolved, and holding the pen without using it.

The method isn't gone. It's waiting on a decision that hasn't been said out loud. Bring one small thing to a person and let them answer — the exchange is what keeps you honest about what you actually know. Standing still reads as neutral and isn't the same as being neutral. The push back is toward deciding again, small enough to finish, so the same steady attention gets something to run on instead of holding a question you already answered.
cells.sheetLine: You know something and you've stopped deciding with it.
cells.verb: deciding by method, committing to the answer your own practice has already tested
cells.place: at a worktable where a direction gets chosen and held

cells.tense: You are already running the method here, and the pen sits down while you talk about it as if it ran itself.
cells.ask: Say 'I decided this' about the timeline or the pressure, wherever you've been calling it out of your hands.
cells.core:
You're already navigating questions with the method — in how you frame the option, what you test, what you wave off. The discipline is running the room, and you describe it as circumstances. It isn't the situation choosing. It's you.

When this sits right, practice runs without force: solitude connects rather than isolates, and the refining serves growth instead of worry. That's the version underneath. What's happened here is that the deciding is real and unclaimed, so it reads as weight instead of something you did. Say it was you, and today's small moves start to feel like yours. No life story needed — one honest assignment of cause.

attempts.check: The record gives a tight operational span and a Body-house, inner-horizon card; it never says what the person's practice actually is, so every cell keeps the verb open and names no field. A reader could fairly say the method they'd guard isn't other people's — the ask in Too Much doesn't settle that, it just spends one answer on an experiment. The sentence serving the writer is 'you have already chosen the one that holds', because it keeps the door open, while the act of committing one direction out loud carries the cell either way. The ask survives being wrong: saying one check out loud is cheap and only finishes the commit.
